reasoning_summary: 0001: Statement of the claim (a tree T has at most one perfect matching); no inference to check, well-posed and vacuously fine if T has no perfect matching. 0002: Blank line, nothing to judge. 0003: Header 'My Proof'; no content. 0004: Blank line, nothing to judge. 0005: Justified setup — assume M and M' are perfect matchings of T=(V,E); proving M=M' is exactly the right way to establish 'at most one'. 0006: The single substantive step, and it is correct in substance though sloppily worded. (a) G=(V, M u M') is a subgraph of T since M,M' are subsets of E — justified. (b) Since M and M' are perfect matchings, every vertex is incident to exactly one M-edge and exactly one M'-edge, so every vertex has degree 1 or 2 in G (degree 1 exactly when the two coincide) — this degree bound is left implicit but is immediate. (c) A graph of maximum degree 2 decomposes into paths and cycles; a path component with at least two edges would have an endpoint v of degree 1, i.e. v's M-edge equals its M'-edge, forcing v's neighbour to be matched twice by the same matching — contradiction. Hence every component is either a single edge lying in M n M' or a cycle. The write-up says 'isolated vertex (which is in M and M')' where it must say 'isolated edge (which is in M and M')': G has no isolated vertices, since perfect matchings cover V. The parenthetical 'which is in M and M'' identifies the object as an edge (a vertex cannot belong to a matching), so this reads as a wording slip rather than a mathematical error, and the intended dichotomy is the correct one. (d) T is acyclic, so G, a subgraph of T, has no cycle; hence every component is a shared edge, giving M ⊆ M' and M' ⊆ M, i.e. M = M'. Justified. 0007: Blank line, nothing to judge. 0008: Meta-request to the reader, not part of the argument. Overall: the argument is sound; the only defects are the 'vertex'/'edge' misnomer in 0006 and the unstated (but routine) degree-≤2 / path-exclusion justification, neither of which breaks the proof.
